title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
claim: Aggregate quality scores fail to separate trained from randomized models across depth, so the metric cannot show learned computation.
layout: 8 small ROC panels in 2x4 grid, shared legend with AUC values
description: A 2x4 grid of ROC-curve subplots titled 'Fuzz ROC Curves (100M tokens)', one panel per layer (1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29). Each panel plots true positive rate against false positive rate, with a dashed diagonal marking chance. Five curves appear in every panel: a gray trained model, blue and orange randomized variants, a green step-0 model, and a black control. The control hugs the diagonal. The gray, blue, orange and green curves bow toward the top-left and mostly overlap. In later layers the randomized curves sit slightly above the trained one. A boxed legend along the bottom lists each curve with its AUC (trained 0.79, control 0.50, randomized 0.87, step 0 0.88). The eye goes first to the separation between the black diagonal and the cluster of colored curves.
caption: `Fuzzing' ROC curve vs. layer for Pythia-6.9b (100 latents sampled per SAE). The trained model (gray line) and randomized variants (colored) overlap, whereas the control (black) is near chance (dotted). This suggests aggregate AUROC alone is insufficient to attribute latents to learned computation. See Figure [ref] for other metrics/model sizes and Appendix [ref] for multiple random seeds.
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
